summary: Defines the Datamover Architecture for iSCSI, an abstract model separating the movement of data between iSCSI endpoints from the rest of the protocol so iSCSI can adapt to new transports. It does not define a specific protocol. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Splits the job of carrying data from the job of giving orders, so new carriers can be used.

questions: what are operational primitives in iscsi
subtitle: A model that lets iSCSI hand the job of moving data to a separate layer, so it can run over RDMA-style transports.

tldr.problem: In classic iSCSI the protocol layer paces and carries every piece of SCSI data itself, which cannot take advantage of technologies that place data straight into the remote buffer.
tldr.mechanism: DA splits out a Datamover layer under iSCSI and defines a small set of Operational Primitives (down calls and up calls) that the two layers use to talk inside one end node.
tldr.outcome: DA is an architecture, not a wire protocol: it defines no Datamover protocol itself. RFC 5047 is Informational and was later updated by RFC 7146.

facts.label: Data integrity floor
facts.value: At least that of the CRC32C data digest

today: RFC 5047 is an Informational RFC and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 7146. It defines an architecture only; concrete Datamover protocols are defined in separate documents.

sections.title: Why Separate Data Movement
sections.content:
The Internet Small Computer System Interface (iSCSI) carries SCSI storage commands over TCP/IP. RFC 3720 gives iSCSI a detailed data transfer model built from SCSI Data-In, SCSI Data-Out and R2T PDUs, and in that model the iSCSI layer itself paces and performs the transfer.

Newer technologies called RDMA and RDDP let one end node place data directly in the final buffer on the remote node. That removes a receive-side copy, saves memory bandwidth and reduces the reassembly buffers needed. RFC 5047 proposes that iSCSI delegate most of the data transfer role to a separate layer designed only to move data, so iSCSI is shielded from the low-level mechanics and only learns when the transfer is done.

DA is motivated by RDMA over TCP/IP but does not depend on RDMA. It is meant as a generic framework for Datamovers built on different RDMA and transport protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Today the same worker gives the orders and carries every box. DA lets a specialist carry the boxes while the worker just waits to hear it is finished.

sections.title: Layering and Scope
sections.content:
DA puts a Datamover layer between the iSCSI layer and the network protocols. The boundary between them is the Datamover Interface (DI). The RFC's example stack puts RDMAP/DDP/MPA over TCP below the Datamover, but stresses that DA is oblivious to whatever sits below the Datamover layer.

The document is deliberately limited. It defines what a Datamover layer and protocol are, how functions are split between the iSCSI and Datamover layers, and how the two interact for each iSCSI PDU. It defines no new Datamover wire protocol and no change to the iSCSI wire protocol. It states that one example of a Datamover protocol is iSER.

Among the stated design ideas: the Datamover can be implemented in hardware or software, DA aims for minimal changes to existing iSCSI implementations, and the notion of an iSCSI session stays entirely within the iSCSI layer.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book only covers how the manager and the crew hand over work. It does not say what kind of truck the crew drives.

sections.title: Core Concepts and Datamover Requirements
sections.content:
DA sorts iSCSI PDUs into two classes. Data-type PDUs (SCSI Data-In and R2T) cause a data transfer that is transparent to the remote iSCSI layer, and the PDU itself is never delivered as-is to it. Control-type PDUs are everything else, including SCSI Data-Out carrying unsolicited data, and travel to the peer unchanged. Solicited SCSI Data-Out is not requested across the interface at all.

Three information elements recur. A Data_Descriptor describes an iSCSI/SCSI data buffer, for example a scatter-gather list. A Connection_Handle identifies an iSCSI connection and is unique for a given pair of iSCSI and Datamover layer instances; it is not the iSCSI Connection Identifier (CID). An Operational Primitive is an abstract call that asks the other layer to act or tells it about an event, with its qualifiers listed like function arguments.

A Datamover protocol MUST provide seven functions, including transporting control-type PDUs as-is, placing SCSI data into the iSCSI layer's I/O buffers, returning data acknowledgements on request, notifying the iSCSI layer asynchronously when a transfer completes or the connection ends, and giving error-free, reliable, in-order delivery with at least the data integrity assurance of the CRC32C iSCSI data digest.
sections.plainLanguage: Some boxes are just carried by the crew and the manager never touches them. Other boxes are letters the manager really reads. Each job has a name tag so nothing gets mixed up.

sections.title: How the Layers Interact
sections.content:
The model follows an iSCSI connection through three stages. In startup, Login runs as defined in RFC 3720, with no Datamover help. If both sides agree, the connection then becomes Datamover-assisted: the iSCSI layer calls Allocate_Connection_Resources and then Enable_Datamover. In the Full Feature Phase all iSCSI communication goes through the Datamover. At wrap-up, Connection_Terminate frees resources.

The iSCSI layer makes nine down calls: Send_Control, Put_Data, Get_Data, Allocate_Connection_Resources, Deallocate_Connection_Resources, Enable_Datamover, Connection_Terminate, Notice_Key_Values and Deallocate_Task_Resources. A target uses Put_Data to send read data and Get_Data to fetch write data. It must call Deallocate_Task_Resources for each task ended without a SCSI Response, such as an aborted task.

The Datamover layer makes four up calls: Control_Notify (a control-type PDU arrived), Connection_Terminate_Notify (the connection failed or ended without iSCSI involvement, for example a TCP reset), Data_Completion_Notify and Data_ACK_Notify. The Datamover layer delivers only control-type PDUs to the iSCSI layer; an initiator infers the arrival of Data-In from the later SCSI Response.
sections.plainLanguage: The manager has a short list of buttons to press for the crew (send this, fetch that, clean up) and the crew has a few bells to ring back (a letter came, a job is done, the road is closed).

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DA separates control from data inside an end node, but it does not allow control and data to travel on different transport media. The ordering and task rules of RFC 3720 are unchanged, so the iSCSI security text in RFC 3723 applies directly to a DA-enabled implementation.

The resource model adds one risk: an implementation that allocates Datamover resources too early could be exposed to denial-of-service attacks. If the Login Phase includes a SecurityNegotiation stage, an iSCSI end node MUST defer calling Allocate_Connection_Resources to the LoginOperationalNegotiation stage, so allocation happens after authentication.

DA defines no wire protocol, so it adds no wire-protocol security issues itself. Each Datamover protocol must document its own, and designers are strongly recommended to consult RFC 5042.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not hand out a crew truck to a stranger at the door. Wait until you have checked who they are.
